title: Labour Economics
tagline: Labour supply and demand, equilibrium and minimum wages, human capital and the returns to education, compensating differentials, discrimination, wage inequality, unions and migration, and job search
summary: Most people’s income comes from work, so the labour market matters for nearly everyone. This course studies how labour supply and demand determine wages and employment; how people invest in education and skills; why wages differ between jobs and between groups; the effects of minimum wages, unions and migration; and how job search shapes unemployment — always confronting theory with empirical evidence.

chapters.title: Labour supply
chapters.summary: The labour–leisure model, income and substitution effects, participation decisions and evidence on labour-supply elasticities.

chapters.title: Labour demand
chapters.summary: Labour demand in the short and long run, the elasticity of factor demand, and the effects of technology and automation.

chapters.title: Labour market equilibrium and minimum wages
chapters.summary: Competitive equilibrium, monopsony, and the theory and evidence on minimum wages.

chapters.title: Human capital and the returns to education
chapters.summary: The schooling decision, human capital versus signalling, and estimating the returns to education.

chapters.title: Compensating wage differentials
chapters.summary: Hedonic wages, the value of a statistical life and the pricing of job amenities.

chapters.title: Discrimination in the labour market
chapters.summary: Taste-based and statistical discrimination, decomposing wage gaps, and audit and correspondence studies.

chapters.title: Wage inequality
chapters.summary: The rise in wage inequality, skill-biased and task-based technical change, and the roles of trade and institutions.

chapters.title: Unions, bargaining and migration
chapters.summary: Collective bargaining and union wage effects, and the economics of immigration and its effects on the labour market.

chapters.title: Job search and unemployment
chapters.summary: Search theory and reservation wages, the Diamond–Mortensen–Pissarides matching model, and unemployment insurance.
